notes.meaning: These verses describe who is truly happy, or "blessed." Blessed people are blameless, which here means honest and sincere, not pretending to be better than they are. They live by God's word and seek God with their whole heart, not a heart split between God and the world. They "do no iniquity" in the sense that they do not make a habit of sin, even though they still struggle with it.

differ.view: No one on earth obeys God perfectly. God's people are called blessed because their sins are freely forgiven, and they keep needing his mercy because their uprightness is never complete.

"Blameless" can be read as "the perfect ones": people who sincerely believe God and whose hearts and lives are ruled by love and obedience. Clarke's outline of verse 3 even speaks of not sinning at all once the heart is fully made holy by Christ living in it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars date this psalm long after David, around the time of the exile in Babylon or later. Keil & Delitzsch picture its writer as a young believer who was being persecuted, perhaps even in prison.

notes.meaning: From here on the psalm becomes a prayer spoken to God. God has commanded his rules, so obeying them is not optional. "Diligently" means carefully and wholeheartedly, not in a careless, hit-or-miss way. God never commands what his grace cannot help us do.

The writer sighs, "Oh, that my ways were steady in obeying you!" This wish is really a prayer: he admits he falls short and asks God to help him. If he paid attention to all of God's commands, he would have nothing to be ashamed of. He means all of them, not only the easy ones, so that he knowingly holds on to no sin and neglects no duty.

He promises to praise God with an honest heart as he learns God's right ways. Like all believers, he is still a student in God's school. He can learn only because God teaches him, so the praise belongs to God.

He firmly decides to obey, and then at once he prays. He knows he cannot keep his promise on his own strength. God may seem to step back from his people for a while, but the prayer is that he will never leave them completely.

How can a young person live a clean life? The answer is to watch your life carefully and check it against God's word. Young people face strong temptations and have little experience, but what is said here is true for anyone. The Bible is the map, and we must keep our eyes on it.
He has sought God with all his heart. Even so, he knows he could drift away, so he asks God to keep him from wandering. The more a person enjoys obeying God, the more afraid he is of straying.

"Hidden" means stored up like treasure, kept safe in the heart. Then the word is ready when temptation comes. Jesus did the same when he answered Satan with "It is written." A word that lives deep inside us is strong protection against sin.

He begins by praising God and then asks to be taught. God is the source of every blessing, so the writer asks for this blessing from him: "teach me your rules." Our prayers should be mixed with praise.
He has spoken God's words out loud to other people. What fills the heart comes out of the mouth. People who are fed by God's word should feed others with it too.
Following God's ways has made him as happy as great wealth would. He is not boasting. He wants to show others that God's word is worth more than the world's riches.

To meditate means to think about something slowly and deeply. He promises to think hard about God's commands, keep his eyes on God's ways, take delight in them, and never forget them. Thinking leads to delight, and delight helps us remember. Good thoughts are only worth something if they lead to good actions.

He asks God to be generous to him, his servant. If God gave us only what we deserve, we would all die, so even being alive is God's kindness. He wants to live not for riches or fun but so that he can keep God's word.

He asks God to open his eyes to the wonderful things in God's law. By nature we are blind to the things of God. The Bible is plain enough, but our hearts are darkened by sin and need the light of the Holy Spirit. He is not asking for new messages, only to see clearly what God has already said.
He feels like a traveller in a strange land, because heaven is his true home. Someone far from home needs a guide, and God's commands are that guide. So he asks God not to hide them from him.
He longs for God's word so strongly that his soul feels crushed by the longing. This is not a passing mood but a steady hunger "at all times." A believer needs God's word the way the body needs food.

God scolds and opposes proud people who wander from his commands, and they fall under his curse. Pride lies at the bottom of every sin we choose on purpose. Seeing this made the writer hold on to God's word even more tightly.

People were mocking him and treating him with contempt, and he asks God to roll that weight off him. Unkind words do not break bones, but they hurt a tender heart. He was being mocked because he obeyed God, so he can bring his case to God.

Even powerful rulers met together to speak against him. Instead of fighting back with words, he kept thinking about God's word. Matthew Henry notes that in this David pictures Christ, whom rulers also turned against.

While rulers plotted against him, God's word cheered him up and told him what to do. Literally, God's teachings are "the men of my counsel," like trusted advisers. If we want God's word to be our joy, we must also let it advise us.

"My soul clings to the dust" pictures someone lying low. It may mean he is close to death, or that his heart is weighed down by earthly desires. He asks God to "quicken" him, which means to give him new life. He asks this "according to your word," that is, as God has promised.
He told God everything about his life: his plans, his troubles, and his sins. God listened and answered him. Now he does not ask God to show him the future, only to teach him what is right to do.

He asks God to help him truly understand the way of God's commands. Then he will think about God's wonderful works and speak of them. We can speak best about God's wonders, especially his saving love, when we understand his ways and walk in them.
His soul is melting with sorrow, like tears dripping or a candle wasting away. He asks God to make him strong "according to your word." God's promise is that he will give us strength for each day.

He asks God to keep him from the path of lying. Matthew Henry notes that David had lied when he was in danger, to Ahimelech and to Achish, and he did not want to fall into that again. He also asks God kindly to give him his law, written on his heart and not only on paper. God's law is a gift of his grace.
